title: Statistical mechanics of classical fractons on a line
authors: Ylias Sadki, Abhishodh Prakash, S. L. Sondhi
abstract: We study the equilibrium statistical mechanics of one-dimensional classical Machian fractons: particles whose dynamics conserves a global dipole moment and whose Hamiltonian couples momentum differences through a position-dependent pair-inertia kernel. Compactly supported interaction kernels have a divergence in the Gibbs partition function, and have been shown to break ergodicity and symmetry by forming non-equilibrium steady states with particle clusters, evading the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner-Coleman theorem. In this paper, we consider kernels with non-compact support and study their ergodic properties. For exponentially decaying kernels, graph-Laplacian and matrix-tree bounds provide an extensive free energy suggesting that a putative statistical mechanical description is valid. Similarly, uniform non-local kernels have a super-extensive free energy and require a Kac rescaling. A generalized Hohenberg--Mermin--Wagner--Coleman argument, supported by finite-size scaling, implies symmetry-breaking density order parameter vanishes at all wave vectors melting the long-range translation-breaking density order of compact kernels. To study the resulting equilibrium ensemble, we construct a nonreversible event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithm that samples the coupled position-momentum phase space while preserving the dipole moment and total momentum. The ECMC sampling is shown to quantitatively match long time-averaged quantites in Hamiltonian dynamics. The equilibrium liquid exhibits preferred short-range clustering and strongly non-Gaussian single-particle momentum tails associated with the correlated nature of positions and momenta. This paper provides a detailed investigation into the equilibrium liquid properties of the non-compact regime, whilst the companion paper investigates the mechanisms that relax the liquid.
summary: This work analyzes the statistical mechanics of classical fractons interacting via pair-inertia kernels, distinguishing between compact and non-compact interaction supports. Using advanced simulation techniques like ECMC and theoretical bounds, the authors establish that non-compact interactions lead to a stable, liquid-like equilibrium state, contrasting sharply with the ordered phases predicted by compact kernels.
main_problem: The paper investigates the equilibrium statistical mechanics of classical fractons, focusing specifically on the behavior when the interaction kernels are non-compact.
main_result: For non-compact kernels, the system reaches an equilibrium liquid state characterized by short-range clustering and non-Gaussian momentum tails, unlike the ordered states found with compact kernels.
method: The authors employ theoretical bounds (Graph-Laplacian, matrix-tree) to determine free energy scaling and use a nonreversible event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithm to sample the coupled position-momentum phase space.
model_or_system: The model consists of one-dimensional classical Machian fractons interacting via a pair-inertia kernel K(x), conserving a global dipole moment and total momentum. The Hamiltonian couples momentum differences through this kernel.
key_observables: Structure factor S(k), single-particle momentum distribution P(p), and the density-wave order parameter.
important_parameters: The nature of the interaction kernel K(x) (compact vs. exponentially decaying vs. uniformly non-decaying) and the system density $ho$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a normalizable Gibbs ensemble for non-compact kernels, and the ECMC sampling is shown to match long-time averages of Hamiltonian dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate representative kernels (Fig. 1) and show the structure factor S(k) and momentum distribution P(p) for the equilibrium liquid state (Fig. 7).
paper_structure: The paper first contrasts compact vs. non-compact kernels, establishing the theoretical framework for free energy scaling. It then develops the ECMC algorithm to sample the equilibrium ensemble, culminating in the characterization of the resulting liquid state properties.
why_interesting: The study of non-equilibrium steady states and the rigorous derivation of equilibrium ensembles for complex interacting particle systems, especially those exhibiting exotic symmetries or constraints, is highly relevant to understanding quantum many-body dynamics.
